title: ORCA Memory Graph Migration Roadmap

format_decision.reason: The migration should be claimable by ABC/PlanRuntime and remain separate from implementation commits until an operator Go is given.

name_contract.meaning: ORCA is the long-term memory graph and context atlas for Odysseus. It owns retrieval, source provenance, derived indexes, query answers, graph readiness, and Lens handoffs.
name_contract.naming_rule: New memory graph work must use ORCA naming. Existing Obsidian names are legacy aliases only until compatibility windows close.

goal: Move the current Obsidian-centered memory graph work into a durable ORCA Memory Graph architecture so Obsidian can be removed from project naming after a compatibility window.

planning_done_means: A canonical ORCA roadmap exists with phases, stop rules, non-goals, risks, gates, expected tests, and ABC ownership.
Alice has a read-only wording/naming task and Bob has a read-only technical boundary task.
Charlie has a heartbeat to integrate Alice/Bob handoffs without starting code migration.
migration_done_means: ORCA is the canonical runtime/API/tool/data/env naming surface for memory graph functions.
Legacy Obsidian routes, tools, env vars, docs, and data paths either redirect through compatibility adapters or are deleted after deprecation gates.
Obsidian is no longer required as a project concept; Markdown/local vault support is expressed as a source or Lens under ORCA.
All focused and integration tests pass under ORCA names, with legacy compatibility tests passing until their scheduled removal.

specs/roadmaps/private-data-memory-ingestion-roadmap.v1.json tracks private corpus and planning memory ingestion.
This ORCA roadmap is a naming and architecture migration plan; it should not replace live activation or ingestion plans.

architecture_decisions.decision: ORCA becomes the canonical memory graph identity; Obsidian becomes a legacy compatibility alias and, later, an optional source/Lens/import concept.
architecture_decisions.why: The current plugin already contains memory graph, retrieval, readiness, RAPTOR, query, and Lens surfaces that are broader than Obsidian.

architecture_decisions.decision: Add ORCA surfaces in parallel before removing Obsidian names.
architecture_decisions.why: Tests, routes, tool contracts, feature flags, and user workflows currently depend on Obsidian names.

architecture_decisions.decision: Extract or introduce the ORCA core contract before doing frontend Lens renames.
architecture_decisions.why: The frontend is large and should consume stable ORCA contracts rather than define the architecture by string replacement.

architecture_decisions.decision: Do not rename vault/data directories until adapters, backups, and rollback tests exist.
architecture_decisions.why: Data path renames are higher risk than API/tool aliases and can strand user vaults.

architecture_decisions.decision: Keep Obsidian user-facing text until ORCA aliases, routes, env vars, and compatibility tests exist.
architecture_decisions.why: Alice identified that premature text removal would promise ORCA before the runtime contracts exist.

architecture_decisions.decision: Treat the Local Markdown Vault as a source adapter under ORCA, not as the ORCA core.
architecture_decisions.why: Bob's boundary audit separates memory graph/retrieval/readiness ownership from filesystem-backed Markdown storage and legacy .obsidian metadata.

non_goals: No code movement, route rename, feature flag flip, live deploy, vault mutation, or data path migration during this planning-only slice.
No deletion of plugins/obsidian until ORCA compatibility surfaces are proven and downstream callers are migrated.
No RAPTOR rebuild, provider calls, Nextcloud transfer, or live server action as part of naming migration planning.
No raw private note content, secrets, tokens, chat IDs, or provider output in roadmap evidence.
No attempt to solve the full 100GB ingestion roadmap inside this ORCA naming roadmap.

risks.risk: Renaming obsidian_* tools or /api/plugins/obsidian routes too early could break bridge contracts, MCP suggestions, and frontend calls.
risks.mitigation: Introduce orca_* aliases and /api/plugins/orca routes first; keep legacy tests green until a scheduled removal phase.

risks.risk: A broad search-and-replace would blur vault/source names, memory graph names, data paths, and operator text.
risks.mitigation: Classify each occurrence as core, lens, source, compatibility, env, data path, docs, or test before editing.

risks.risk: Changing data/obsidian_vaults or .obsidian metadata paths prematurely could orphan existing user data.
risks.mitigation: Keep data-path migration late, explicit, backed up, and reversible.

risks.risk: ORCA migration could conflict with live activation and private ingestion roadmaps.
risks.mitigation: Treat this roadmap as a naming/architecture track; live activation and ingestion remain separate parent/peer tracks.

stop_rules: Stop on foreign staged files, secrets, token leakage, private raw content, or hotfile conflicts.
Stop if a slice would require destructive git, history rewrite, live deploy, live route probe, env mutation, or vault/data migration without explicit operator Go.
Stop if an implementation slice tries to remove legacy Obsidian names before ORCA aliases and compatibility tests exist.
Stop if test impact cannot be scoped to explicit bridge, route, tool, frontend, and memory readiness contracts.
Stop if Alice or Bob reports overlap with the existing live activation or private data ingestion roadmaps that changes migration priority.

release_go_language.go: Proceed to implementation only after Alice and Bob handoffs agree on naming boundaries, technical cut lines, compatibility windows, and focused tests.
release_go_language.partial: Proceed with docs/glossary and ORCA alias tests only; defer code movement and data path changes.
release_go_language.no_go: Do not implement if compatibility risk is unclear, active roadmap conflicts exist, or tests would require broad brittle rewrites.
release_go_language.deferred: Keep Obsidian names as legacy longer when external callers or live deployments still depend on them.
